Harnessing Multimodal Large Language Models for Training-Free Human-Object Interaction Detection

Zhaolin Cai   Huiyu Duan   Liu Yang   Yanjun Qin Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Affiliation: Xinjiang University    Bo Ai   Wei Chen   Xiongkuo Min   Guangtao Zhai ††thanks: Corresponding authors. Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Affiliation: Beijing Jiaotong University Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory
Abstract

Human-object interaction (HOI) detection aims to localize human-object pairs and recognize their interactions. Traditional supervised methods perform strongly but rely on task-specific training. Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer a promising route to training-free HOI detection through their broad visual-semantic knowledge and versatile perceptual and reasoning capabilities. However, existing approaches largely invoke these capabilities through loosely coordinated inference stages. This fragmented execution restricts the role of interaction hypotheses in guiding visual exploration, leaving key participants overlooked and local ambiguities unresolved. Furthermore, propagating early semantic assumptions through subsequent visual grounding and relation prediction induces self-reinforcing semantic circularity. To resolve these challenges, we propose HarnessHOI, a training-free framework that transforms passive MLLM inference into an active interaction-centric harness. Specifically, we introduce an interaction-guided perception mechanism that projects emerging interaction hypotheses back into the visual space to discover missing participants and refine ambiguous evidence through targeted observation. Furthermore, a relation-agnostic geometric adjudication module reconciles multi-source evidence to establish a unified spatial basis for grounded interaction reasoning across multiple actions and semantic roles. Extensive experiments on HICO-DET and V-COCO demonstrate that HarnessHOI achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed harness for complex interaction understanding. Code will be released upon publication.

1 Introduction

Human-object interaction (HOI) detection aims to localize human-object pairs and recognize the interactions between them, typically represented as ⟨human,action,object⟩\langle\mathrm{human},\mathrm{action},\mathrm{object}\rangle triplets (Chao et al., 2018; Gupta and Malik, 2015). As a foundational task for scene understanding, it supports applications ranging from visual surveillance (Dogariu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024) to embodied AI (Mascaro et al., 2023; Bahl et al., 2023). Traditional supervised methods have achieved strong performance by learning task-specific interaction representations and prediction functions from HOI annotations (Gkioxari et al., 2018; Liao et al., 2022). However, their reliance on extensive annotations and dedicated training limits their scalability to the compositional and long-tailed interaction space encountered in real-world scenes (Hou et al., 2020; Hou et al., 2021).

Recent vision-language models and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially expanded their ability to visual understanding and visual-semantic knowledge (Radford et al., 2021; Bai et al., 2025). Initial approaches integrate this knowledge into HOI detectors through feature alignment, prompt adaptation, or supervised optimization (Lei et al., 2024b; Lei et al., 2024a). Recent work further develops part-aware interaction representations (Tonini et al., 2026) and unifies HOI detection with generation (Yang et al., 2026). Although effective, these approaches still require specific training, reintroducing the annotation and optimization burden that foundation models are expected to alleviate. Training-free paradigms therefore directly exploit frozen pretrained models for interaction grounding and prediction. Retrieval-based approaches score candidate interactions against visual-semantic knowledge (Tonini et al., 2025), while the variant formulates recognition as candidate-conditioned semantic assessment (Xuan et al., 2026). Recent agentic methods further revisit candidate interactions and recover visual entities through multi-stage semantic reasoning (Lei et al., 2026). Despite this progress, existing approaches leave semantic reasoning and visual perception through a separate process, leaving perception passive to the emerging interaction hypotheses.

Human-object relations are fundamentally constrained by both relational semantics and fine-grained visual evidence distributed across the scene (Wang et al., 2019; Wan et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2023).An emerging interaction hypothesis provides cues to recover overlooked participants or resolve local visual ambiguity. Conversely, grounded visual evidence provides necessary spatial constraints to verify candidate relations. Existing methods fail to regulate this reciprocal dependency, resulting in two coupled limitations. First, visual perception remains static when emerging interaction hypotheses are not systematically projected back into the image space to guide observation. This creates perceptual passivity, leaving missing entities and ambiguous regions unresolved. Second, directly propagating semantic proposals through visual grounding and subsequent relation evaluation induces semantic circularity, where initial semantic assumptions bias the visual interpretation and produce self-reinforcing predictions and spurious relational judgments. The central challenge is therefore to harness the complementary semantic and perceptual capabilities of MLLMs within a unified framework, enabling interaction hypotheses to actively guide visual exploration while grounding the resulting judgments in instance-level visual evidence.

To address these limitations, we propose HarnessHOI, a training-free framework that transforms MLLM interpretation into an active interaction-centric harness paradigm(Figure 1). To overcome perceptual passivity, HarnessHOI incorporates interaction-guided perception that projects emerging hypotheses back into image space, actively discovering interaction participants and requesting targeted observations for ambiguous evidence. To mitigate semantic circularity, relation-agnostic geometric adjudication reconciles the resulting localization candidates under persistent instance identities, establishing a unified visual grounding according to participant evidence. Grounded interaction reasoning then assesses multiple actions and semantic roles using these shared groundings and the acquired visual evidence. Together, these mechanisms establish an interaction-centric harness that coordinates interaction-guided evidence acquisition with relation-agnostic visual grounding, enabling coherent and reliable training-free HOI prediction with frozen MLLMs.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We present HarnessHOI, a training-free framework that harnesses complementary perceptual and semantic capabilities of frozen MLLMs for HOI detection, moving beyond isolated semantic scoring or loosely coupled multi-stage reasoning.

  • •

    We introduce interaction-guided perception, relation-agnostic geometric adjudication, and grounded interaction reasoning to connect hypothesis-driven visual exploration with shared participant groundings and evidence-grounded relation assessment, addressing perceptual passivity and semantic circularity.

  • •

    Extensive experiments on HICO-DET and V-COCO demonstrate that HarnessHOI achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods, validating the effectiveness of the proposed interaction-centric harness for human-object interaction detection.

2 Related Work

2.1 Traditional Human-Object Interaction Detection

Traditional human-object interaction (HOI) detection frameworks primarily rely on fully supervised paradigms, which are broadly grouped into two-stage pipelines and single-stage set-prediction architectures (Zhang et al., 2021a; Zhang et al., 2022b). Two-stage methods detect human and object proposals prior to classifying interaction predicates (Gao et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021b; Zhang et al., 2022a). Conversely, single-stage transformer architectures utilize learnable queries to directly decode relation triplets from global visual contexts (Kim et al., 2021; Zou et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021; Tamura et al., 2021). To improve generalization across unseen combinations, recent work incorporates pretrained vision-language representations by aligning visual features with text embeddings (Yuan et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2023; Ning et al., 2023; Mao et al., 2023). Although these supervised methods achieve competitive performance on closed-world benchmarks, they remain inherently constrained by task-specific parameter optimization and heavy reliance on exhaustive triplet annotations, impeding their scalability to open-world scenarios.

2.2 Foundation Models for HOI Detection

The evolution of vision-language models and multimodal large language models offers expansive visual-semantic knowledge, prompting a shift toward parameter-efficient and training-free HOI detection. Early adaptation strategies align interaction representations with pretrained visual-semantic knowledge (Wu et al., 2023; Cao et al., 2023; Lei et al., 2025a). Recent methods learn part-aware representations (Tonini et al., 2026), distill MLLM knowledge into HOI detectors (Gao et al., 2025), or unify detection and generation (Yang et al., 2026). Supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning further adapt MLLMs for interaction reasoning (Wu et al., 2026b). Although effective, these approaches still require specific optimization. Training-free methods therefore directly exploit frozen foundation models for interaction prediction. Visual-semantic retrieval approaches calculate similarity scores between representations and text embeddings (Tonini et al., 2025). The variant formulates HOI detection as candidate-conditioned generation (Xuan et al., 2026). Recent agentic frameworks introduce multi-agent and multi-turn reasoning to propose and revisit candidate interactions prior to visual grounding (Wang et al., 2026; Lei et al., 2026). Despite these advancements, current training-free paradigms treat semantic reasoning and visual grounding as isolated steps. As a result, visual perception remains fundamentally passive to initial semantic hypotheses, leaving models susceptible to perceptual omission and semantic circularity.

2.3 MLLM Harnessing for Visual Reasoning

Active perception principles advocate dynamically adapting visual observation based on task demands rather than relying on static image features Bajcsy (1988). Recent vision-language research operationalizes active perception by incorporating selective region re-encoding or localized attention mechanisms during MLLM inference Zhang et al. (2025a); Shalam et al. (2026). In parallel, agentic workflows decompose complex visual tasks into sequential reasoning and grounding operations Lei et al. (2026). However, existing active harnessing strategies are primarily designed for free-form visual question answering or coarse region grounding, lacking effective and controllable mechanisms to manage complex relational understanding inherent to HOI detection. Applying generic workflows directly to HOI detection allows unconstrained semantic assumptions to distort visual search. HarnessHOI overcomes these limitations by unifying interaction-guided perception with relational reasoning, enabling a controlled harnessing paradigm that prevents semantic bias while maintaining rigorous spatial and relational grounding.

3 Method

3.1 Interaction-Centric HOI Harness

HarnessHOI introduces an interaction-centric harness in which semantic hypotheses guide participant acquisition and the acquired evidence supports grounded relation assessment (Figure 2). Shared participant identities connect these operations across multiple actions and semantic roles, allowing evidence acquired under one hypothesis to support further interaction judgments.

Problem formulation.

Given an image II and an interaction taxonomy 𝒯\mathcal{T}, our goal is to predict a scored set of grounded interactions 𝒴^={(k,s⁡(k))}\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}=\{(k,s(k))\}. Each entity ei=(i,bi,ci)∈ℰe_{i}=(i,b_{i},c_{i})\in\mathcal{E} comprises an image-level identity, a normalized bounding box, and a category. An interaction k=(h,a,o)k=(h,a,o) associates a human h∈ℋ⊆ℰh\in\mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathcal{E} with an action aa and a target o∈ℰo\in\mathcal{E} under the semantics of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. The score s⁡(k)s(k) expresses visual support for the interaction between the localized participants. We denote the MLLM by FθF_{\theta}, with θ\theta fixed throughout inference.

HarnessHOI overview.

As illustrated in Figure 2, HarnessHOI consists of interaction-guided perception, relation-agnostic geometric adjudication, and grounded interaction reasoning. Specifically, we use the interaction hypotheses generated by FθF_{\theta} to guide participant discovery and targeted observation, associating the resulting localization candidates and their source views with persistent instance identities. We then apply relation-agnostic geometric adjudication to select a consistent grounding for each participant according to its identity, category, and visible extent. Based on these shared groundings and the acquired image evidence, grounded interaction reasoning evaluates multiple actions and semantic roles through visual question answering. The same frozen MLLM performs all three stages, with its answer distributions determining geometric selection and interaction scores.

3.2 Interaction-Guided Perception

The semantics of an interaction provide cues to its participating objects and their spatial relation to the human. Interaction-guided perception exploits these cues to recover overlooked participants and obtain local observations for precise instance grounding.

Hypothesis-directed discovery.

Starting from an initial entity set ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} localized by FθF_{\theta} in II, we expand the participant set by querying the model about the visible interactions of each human in ℋ0⊆ℰ0\mathcal{H}_{0}\subseteq\mathcal{E}_{0}. Conditioned on the full image, initial entities, and interaction semantics in 𝒯\mathcal{T}, FθF_{\theta} jointly generates interaction hypotheses, localizations of newly discovered participants, and observation requests:

(𝒫D,Δ​ℰD,ℛ)=Dθ​(I,ℰ0,𝒯),\bigl(\mathcal{P}_{D},\Delta\mathcal{E}_{D},\mathcal{R}\bigr)=D_{\theta}\bigl(I,\mathcal{E}_{0},\mathcal{T}\bigr), (1)

where DθD_{\theta} denotes the discovery operation of FθF_{\theta}. The positive interaction hypotheses define human-target associations 𝒫D\mathcal{P}_{D} over the expanded participant set ℰ0∪Δ​ℰD\mathcal{E}_{0}\cup\Delta\mathcal{E}_{D}, where Δ​ℰD\Delta\mathcal{E}_{D} contains participants newly localized in the full image. For hypotheses involving unlocalized targets or ambiguous instance boundaries, the observation requests ℛ\mathcal{R} specify the relevant image regions and participants for further visual inspection.

Targeted visual observation.

Targeted observation complements global interaction context with local visual evidence of participant identity and extent. Using high-resolution crops acquired from II according to ℛ\mathcal{R}, FθF_{\theta} refines existing localizations and grounds additional participants, conditioned on the requested target description and local instance context. To integrate observations across image scales, we associate candidate localizations with persistent instance identities and express their boxes in image coordinates. The corresponding human-target associations form 𝒫O\mathcal{P}_{O}, connecting humans to the existing targets addressed by their observations and to newly localized participants.

Across initial localization, discovery, and local observation, the shared instance representation organizes visual evidence under NN participant identities. Each identity ii has a candidate localization set ℬi={(bi,m,ci,m,vi,m)}m=1Mi\mathcal{B}_{i}=\{(b_{i,m},c_{i,m},v_{i,m})\}_{m=1}^{M_{i}}. Here bi,mb_{i,m} and ci,mc_{i,m} specify the box and category of candidate mm, and vi,mv_{i,m} identifies its source view. The global image and acquired crops form the shared view set 𝒱\mathcal{V}. The candidate sets {ℬi}i=1N\{\mathcal{B}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} preserve alternative spatial interpretations of each participant for geometric adjudication, while 𝒱\mathcal{V} provides the global context and local detail for grounded interaction reasoning. The observation policy and coordinate handling are detailed in Appendix A.

3.3 Relation-Agnostic Geometric Adjudication

We introduce relation-agnostic geometric adjudication to establish a consistent localization for each participant across its interactions. For each instance, we compare the candidate localizations against the shared views 𝒱\mathcal{V} according to its identity, category, and complete visible extent. This instance-level criterion decouples geometric selection from support for individual actions or roles.

Let xx denote a visual question together with its instance context and image evidence, and ℒx\mathcal{L}_{x} the candidate answer set. We define the normalized support of FθF_{\theta} for an answer ℓ∈ℒx\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{x} as

qθ​(ℓ∣x)=exp⁡(zℓ​(x))∑j∈ℒxexp⁡(zj​(x)),q_{\theta}(\ell\mid x)=\frac{\exp\bigl(z_{\ell}(x)\bigr)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{L}_{x}}\exp\bigl(z_{j}(x)\bigr)}, (2)

where zℓ​(x)z_{\ell}(x) is the output logit of FθF_{\theta} for answer label ℓ\ell. For an instance with Mi>1M_{i}>1, xigeox_{i}^{\mathrm{geo}} contains the comparison question, candidate localizations ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i}, and shared views 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Each answer label ℓi,m\ell_{i,m} identifies a candidate mm, and we select the candidate with the greatest visual support:

mi∗=arg​maxm=1,…,Mi⁡qθ​(ℓi,m∣xigeo).m_{i}^{*}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{m=1,\ldots,M_{i}}q_{\theta}\bigl(\ell_{i,m}\mid x_{i}^{\mathrm{geo}}\bigr). (3)

The selected candidate defines (bi∗,ci∗)=(bi,mi∗,ci,mi∗)(b_{i}^{*},c_{i}^{*})=(b_{i,m_{i}^{*}},c_{i,m_{i}^{*}}); identities with one candidate retain that localization. Collecting these selections yields the grounded entity set ℰ∗={(i,bi∗,ci∗)}i=1N\mathcal{E}^{*}=\{(i,b_{i}^{*},c_{i}^{*})\}_{i=1}^{N}. All relations involving an entity in ℰ∗\mathcal{E}^{*} use its selected box and category, so hypotheses concerning the same participant are evaluated with consistent spatial grounding.

3.4 Grounded Interaction Reasoning

Given the shared instance groundings ℰ∗\mathcal{E}^{*}, we formulate visual questions for candidate interactions using the action or role definitions in 𝒯\mathcal{T}. The frozen MLLM FθF_{\theta} evaluates each question with the global image and relevant local views from 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Pair, action, agent, and binding questions use the answer set ℒrel={false,true,unknown}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}=\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true},\mathrm{unknown}\}, representing rejection, support, and unresolved visual evidence, respectively, with normalized support given by Equation 2.

Candidate pair construction.

The relation candidates draw on both the associations established during perception and the visual evidence across the expanded participant set. Let ℋ∗⊆ℰ∗\mathcal{H}^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{E}^{*} denote the localized humans and 𝒫={(h,o)∈ℋ∗×ℰ∗:h≠o}\mathcal{P}=\{(h,o)\in\mathcal{H}^{*}\times\mathcal{E}^{*}:h\neq o\} the human-entity pairs. For each pair, FθF_{\theta} evaluates whether any positive action or physical role binding in 𝒯\mathcal{T} is visually supported, yielding qFh,oq_{\mathrm{F}}^{h,o}, qTh,oq_{\mathrm{T}}^{h,o}, and qUh,oq_{\mathrm{U}}^{h,o}. These assessments extend the discovery and observation associations to define the candidate pair set:

𝒦\displaystyle\mathcal{K} =𝒫D∪𝒫O∪{(h,o)∈𝒫|qFh,o≤max⁡(qTh,o,qUh,o)}.\displaystyle=\mathcal{P}_{D}\cup\mathcal{P}_{O}\cup\bigl\{(h,o)\in\mathcal{P}\bigm|q_{\mathrm{F}}^{h,o}\leq\max\bigl(q_{\mathrm{T}}^{h,o},q_{\mathrm{U}}^{h,o}\bigr)\bigr\}. (4)

Multi-label action verification.

To recognize multiple interactions involving the same participants, we evaluate each pair in 𝒦\mathcal{K} over its category-compatible action set. The action domain extends beyond the hypotheses used for participant discovery:

𝒬+={(h,a,o)|(h,o)∈𝒦,a∈𝒜+(co∗)},\mathcal{Q}_{+}=\bigl\{(h,a,o)\bigm|(h,o)\in\mathcal{K},\;a\in\mathcal{A}^{+}(c_{o}^{*})\bigr\}, (5)

where 𝒜+​(c)\mathcal{A}^{+}(c) is the set of positive actions associated with category cc in 𝒯\mathcal{T}. For each (h,a,o)∈𝒬+(h,a,o)\in\mathcal{Q}_{+}, xh,a,orelx_{h,a,o}^{\mathrm{rel}} denotes the visual question context for verifying action aa between the selected instances h,oh,o. The interaction score is

s⁡(h,a,o)=qθ​(true∣xh,a,orel).s(h,a,o)=q_{\theta}\bigl(\mathrm{true}\mid x_{h,a,o}^{\mathrm{rel}}\bigr). (6)

Separate normalization over ℒrel\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}} for each action preserves the multi-label nature of HOI.

Compositional role verification.

In semantic-role prediction, action occurrence and the visibility of its target are distinct aspects of the interaction. We extend the prediction to k=(h,a,r,o)k=(h,a,r,o), where rr specifies the semantic role and o∈ℰ∗∪{∅}o\in\mathcal{E}^{*}\cup\{\varnothing\} accommodates physical and null targets. To distinguish target visibility from target identity, we decompose role prediction into action support, conditional target visibility, and instance-specific binding. For a given interaction, we suppress the arguments of the component supports and write

qA\displaystyle q_{A} =qθ​(true∣xh,aagent),\displaystyle=q_{\theta}\bigl(\mathrm{true}\mid x_{h,a}^{\mathrm{agent}}\bigr), (7)
qσ\displaystyle q_{\sigma} =qθ​(σ∣xh,a,rrole),\displaystyle=q_{\theta}\bigl(\sigma\mid x_{h,a,r}^{\mathrm{role}}\bigr),
qB\displaystyle q_{B} =qθ​(true∣xh,a,r,obind),\displaystyle=q_{\theta}\bigl(\mathrm{true}\mid x_{h,a,r,o}^{\mathrm{bind}}\bigr),

where xh,aagentx_{h,a}^{\mathrm{agent}} denotes the context for verifying whether human hh performs action aa. Target visibility is assessed in xh,a,rrolex_{h,a,r}^{\mathrm{role}} conditional on action occurrence, and the binding of oo to role rr is assessed in xh,a,r,obindx_{h,a,r,o}^{\mathrm{bind}} conditional on both action occurrence and target visibility. Action and binding questions use ℒrel\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}, while the role-state answer σ\sigma ranges over ℒrole={missing,visible,unknown}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{role}}=\{\mathrm{missing},\mathrm{visible},\mathrm{unknown}\}, whose outcomes denote the absence of a visible, localizable target, the presence of such a target, and unresolved visual evidence, respectively.

Action and role-state factors cover every human in ℋ∗\mathcal{H}^{*} and all corresponding actions and roles in 𝒯\mathcal{T}, while physical binding factors are evaluated for pairs in 𝒦\mathcal{K}. Writing qMq_{M} and qVq_{V} for the missing and visible supports, we obtain scores for person-level actions k=(h,a)k=(h,a), physical role targets, and null targets:

sagent=qA,sphysical=qA​qV​qB,sNULL=qA​qM.s_{\mathrm{agent}}=q_{A},\qquad s_{\mathrm{physical}}=q_{A}\,q_{V}\,q_{B},\qquad s_{\mathrm{NULL}}=q_{A}\,q_{M}. (8)

We apply the action-triplet formulation to HICO-DET and the semantic-role formulation to V-COCO. For HICO-DET, we additionally evaluate the no​_​interaction\mathrm{no\_interaction} predicate over all pairs in 𝒫\mathcal{P}, using its independently assessed true support as the detection score.

The resulting prediction set 𝒴^\widehat{\mathcal{Y}} couples each interaction score s⁡(k)s(k) with the selected participant boxes from ℰ∗\mathcal{E}^{*}. Participants discovered and observations acquired under individual interaction hypotheses thus contribute to action and role verification across the expanded scene representation. Further details on inference, implementation, and question semantics are provided in Appendices A, B.3, and G.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks and metrics.

We evaluate HarnessHOI on the complete HICO-DET (Chao et al., 2018) and V-COCO (Gupta and Malik, 2015) test sets, containing 9,658 and 4,946 images, respectively. HICO-DET reports Full, Rare, and Non-Rare mAP over 600 HOI categories under Default and Known Object evaluation. Open-vocabulary evaluation follows RF-UC, NF-UC, UO, and UV. V-COCO reports role AP over 25 semantic roles under scenarios S1 and S2. Both benchmarks require participant matching at IoU 0.5. Detailed metric definitions and evaluation protocols appear in Appendix B.

Implementation details.

All perceptual and reasoning operations use a single frozen Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026), with at most two local observations per image. The harness receives the image and public interaction vocabulary. Prompts and inference policy are selected using the official training sets, following the protocol in Appendix B. Inference settings, implementation, and visual questions appear in Appendices A, B.3, and G.

4.2 Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods

Regular settings.

Table 1 compares HarnessHOI with representative task-optimized and training-free HOI detectors. HarnessHOI establishes state-of-the-art training-free performance on both benchmarks. On HICO-DET, it achieves 33.20% Default Full mAP, surpassing AgentHOI (Lei et al., 2026) by 3.59 points and the training-free variant of DA-HOI (Xuan et al., 2026) by 1.70 points, and reaches 36.85% under Known Object evaluation. It also obtains the best training-free Rare and Non-Rare results, with 41.63% Rare mAP exceeding AgentHOI by 1.30 points. The consistent gains across frequency groups and evaluation settings demonstrate the effectiveness of the HOI harness in recognizing common and infrequent interactions.

On V-COCO, HarnessHOI obtains 44.65%/49.70% role AP under S1/S2, surpassing DYSCO (Tonini et al., 2025) by 1.85/1.88 points. The gains under both scenarios demonstrate the effectiveness of the harness in recognizing actions and identifying their corresponding role targets. Extended results, including a common-evaluator comparison with the released predictions of AgentHOI, are provided in Appendix C.

Open-vocabulary settings.

Table 2 reports results under RF-UC, NF-UC, UO, and UV using the same HarnessHOI predictions. The method achieves 40.15%, 33.64%, 35.45%, and 33.87% Unseen mAP, respectively, attaining the best training-free results in all four partitions. Improvements over AgentHOI (Lei et al., 2026) reach 1.75 points on UO and 4.02 points on UV. On NF-UC, HarnessHOI surpasses the strongest previous training-free result, ADA-CM (Lei et al., 2023), by 3.53 points. It also obtains the strongest reported training-free Seen results across all four settings. The simultaneous gains on Unseen and Seen classes demonstrate the effectiveness of the harness across interaction compositions, object categories, and actions. Complete results appear in Appendix C.

4.3 Ablation Studies

We conduct ablation studies to evaluate the overall HOI harness and the contributions of its perceptual and reasoning components. The component studies use the same frozen Qwen3.5-9B and report HICO-DET Default Full mAP and V-COCO S1/S2 role AP on the complete test sets. Detailed settings and complete results are provided in Appendix D.

Effectiveness of the HOI harness.

Table 3 compares the complete HOI harness with direct generation and an initial-instance baseline that verifies relations among initially localized participants. On HICO-DET, the initial-instance baseline achieves 31.45% mAP compared with 15.62% for direct generation, and the complete harness further reaches 33.20%. On V-COCO, the complete harness improves the initial-instance baseline from 42.90%/47.20% to 44.65%/49.70% AP. These results demonstrate that grounded verification strengthens interaction recognition, while interaction-guided perception and geometric adjudication further improve detection through participant discovery and shared grounding. Candidate-ranking analysis and backbone generalization with InternVL3-8B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B are presented in Appendices E.4 and D.6.

Interaction-guided perception.

As shown in Table 3, participant discovery improves V-COCO S2 AP by 0.77 points. Under the same generation budget, interaction-guided discovery outperforms repeated participant localization by 0.75 points in HICO-DET mAP and 0.78/0.82 points in V-COCO AP (Table 4). With region counts and sizes fixed, targeted observation improves over non-directed observation by 0.50 and 0.58/0.62 points, respectively. Interaction semantics therefore provide effective guidance for recovering overlooked participants and observing relevant regions. The coverage analysis in Appendix D.3 further shows how recovered participants contribute to interaction recognition.

Geometric adjudication and interaction reasoning.

Table 4 evaluates relation-agnostic geometric adjudication and grounded interaction reasoning. With candidate boxes and image views fixed, selecting shared groundings according to participant identity, category, and visible extent improves over relation-conditioned adjudication by 0.41 points in HICO-DET mAP and 0.47/0.54 points in V-COCO AP. On identical relation candidates, verification using the selected participants and acquired visual evidence further improves over proposal-conditioned questions by 0.70 and 0.73/0.86 points. Together, these results validate the separation between hypothesis-guided visual exploration and evidence-grounded interaction assessment.

Action and role prediction.

The analyses in Appendix D.5 show that combining perceptual associations with visual pair assessment improves detection, while verifying compatible labels recovers multiple actions involving the same participants. Role prediction further benefits from separately assessing action occurrence, target visibility, and role binding. On identical role candidates, compositional verification improves S1/S2 AP from 41.10%/46.30% to 44.65%/49.70%. With the final true-positive counts unchanged, this improvement reflects more accurate ranking of role predictions through the composition of action and target evidence.

Inference computation.

Table 33 compares detection performance and computational cost using the same frozen MLLM. Compared with direct generation using eight independent responses per image, HarnessHOI improves HICO-DET Full mAP by 13.36 points, while reducing the measured cost from 19.95 to 13.26 GPU-worker seconds per image. On V-COCO, the gains reach 22.44/23.20 points in S1/S2 AP, with measured costs of 22.07 and 20.94 GPU-worker seconds per image for HarnessHOI and repeated generation, respectively. The substantial detection gains at comparable computational cost demonstrate the advantage of coordinating visual exploration and grounded reasoning within the harness. Further computation analyses and hardware measurements are provided in Appendix E.

5 Conclusion

We presented HarnessHOI, a training-free framework that harnesses frozen MLLMs for active interaction-guided perceptual reasoning. Its HOI harness connects interaction understanding with visual exploration, enabling the model to discover overlooked participants and inspect ambiguous regions. Relation-agnostic geometric adjudication reconciles the acquired localization candidates, and grounded interaction reasoning uses the selected instance groundings to verify multiple actions and semantic roles. Extensive experiments on HICO-DET and V-COCO show that HarnessHOI achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods, demonstrating the value of coordinating visual exploration and relation assessment through shared instance groundings.

AI use statement

In the preparation of this work, generative AI tools assisted with the purpose of language polishing and grammar correction to improve clarity and readability. We confirm that all core research ideas, the conceptual framework, experimental design, data analysis are entirely the original work of the authors. The authors take full and sole responsibility for the accuracy, integrity, and all claims made within this work.

Ethics statement

Our work adheres to the ICLR Code of Ethics. The research is conducted exclusively on publicly available, standard academic benchmarks (HICO-DET and V-COCO), which are widely used for evaluating human-object interaction detection algorithms. Our primary motivation is to advance the field for societal benefit, such as assistive robotics and accessible visual understanding. We believe that our framework supports the responsible development of AI by making the visual basis of interaction predictions available for inspection. Specifically, the harness associates discovered participants, targeted observations, and relation assessments with shared groundings, allowing predictions to be examined against the image evidence and corresponding visual questions. Responsible applications should respect privacy, consent, and the original data providers’ terms, while accounting for biases in pretrained models and benchmark coverage. Human oversight should be appropriate to the consequences of an incorrect prediction. We advocate for the responsible development and deployment of this technology, ensuring its application aligns with ethical principles and contributes positively to human well-being.

Reproducibility statement

We are fully committed to ensuring the complete reproducibility of our research. To this end, we provide a detailed description of our methodology in Section 3, supplemented by the complete inference procedure in Appendix A and the prompt instructions and visual questions in Appendix G. All crucial implementation details, including the frozen Qwen3.5-9B backbone, image processing, inference settings, and evaluation protocols, are clearly documented in Section 4.1 and Appendix B. Our experiments are built on standard public benchmarks and common libraries, including PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, and vLLM, to ensure broad accessibility. Extended comparisons and ablations specify their baseline formulations and controlled variables in Appendices C and D, while Appendix E details the computation measurements and independent-run evaluation. We also pledge to release our source code, inference configurations, image lists, seed assignments, and evaluation scripts upon the publication of this paper, which we believe will allow the community to fully replicate our findings and extend our work.
