Appendix A Additional Details of HarnessHOI

A.1 Shared Participants and Interaction Evidence

Table 5 summarizes how the MLLM performs interaction-guided perception, relation-agnostic geometric adjudication, and grounded interaction reasoning. Throughout these stages, each participant retains a common identity that links its localization candidates to the interactions involving it.

Participant identity.

Each entity eie_{i} has a persistent identity and a candidate set ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i} containing its alternative boxes, categories, and source views. Discovery identifies additional participants and relations among existing participants, while observation supplies local grounding candidates. Geometric adjudication selects the box and category shared by all relations involving the entity.

Initial localization and discovery associate exact category-and-box matches with the same identity. Discovery outputs are merged in human-group order, matching each new localization against the accumulated participant set. Other localized participants receive new identities, while observation refinements retain the identity of the designated participant.

Evidence and associations.

Discovery associations 𝒫D\mathcal{P}_{D} connect humans to the targets of positive interaction hypotheses. Observation associations 𝒫O\mathcal{P}_{O} connect the inspected human to the requested target and newly localized participants. Both contribute candidate pairs for relation verification, where each action or role receives its own visual assessment.

A.2 Interaction-Guided Perception

Initial localization and grouped discovery.

Initial localization groups each person with the identifiable targets involved in their interactions. We then divide the initially localized humans into groups of at most four for discovery. Conditioned on the full image and initial entity set, each group is examined for additional interactions and participants. Newly discovered humans participate in subsequent geometric and relational assessment, while discovery groups are defined by the initial human set.

A hypothesis specifies the human, action, and target identities, together with semantic roles for V-COCO. Each person may participate in multiple actions with multiple targets. Existing targets are referenced by identity, and new participants are localized by category and complete visible extent. A hypothesis with unresolved target localization can request a local observation, specifying the human, target description, action and role, and region to inspect.

Observation selection.

The harness executes at most two observation requests per image. Requests concerning an unlocalized target take precedence over requests to complete an existing participant’s boundary. Within each priority, different humans receive their first observation before a second request for the same human is considered. Requests for the same known target are deduplicated by identity; unresolved targets are distinguished by their associated human and description. Each discovery group may propose two requests, while the image-level budget governs execution after merging.

Given the target description and instances within the requested region, the MLLM refines eligible groundings and localizes additional visible participants. A single observation can therefore provide localization candidates for several participants in the same crop.

Local-to-global geometry.

For a crop with image-pixel boundaries [L,T,R,B][L,T,R,B], let (x,y)(x,y) be a point normalized to [0,1000][0,1000] within the crop. Its image coordinate is

[x′y′]=[LT]+11000​[R−L00B−T]​[xy].\begin{bmatrix}x^{\prime}\\ y^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}L\\ T\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{1000}\begin{bmatrix}R-L&0\\ 0&B-T\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\end{bmatrix}. (9)

Here (x′,y′)(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}) is a full-image pixel position. For an image of size W×HW\times H, (1000​x′/W,1000​y′/H)(1000x^{\prime}/W,1000y^{\prime}/H) gives its normalized coordinates. Both box corners are transformed to this full-image representation before updating the candidate set. An existing identity is eligible for refinement when all its candidate boxes lie within the crop; boundary-crossing instances provide contextual references. Localized boxes cover the visible extent of each instance.

Observation associations.

Let hρh_{\rho} denote the human associated with observation ρ\rho, tρt_{\rho} its known target when available, and ℰρnew\mathcal{E}_{\rho}^{\mathrm{new}} the newly localized identities. For the acquired observations ℛobs\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{obs}}, the corresponding relation associations are

𝒫O=⋃ρ∈ℛobs{(hρ,o):o∈ℰρnew∪{tρ},o≠hρ},\mathcal{P}_{O}=\bigcup_{\rho\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{obs}}}\bigl\{(h_{\rho},o):o\in\mathcal{E}_{\rho}^{\mathrm{new}}\cup\{t_{\rho}\},\ o\neq h_{\rho}\bigr\}, (10)

where {tρ}\{t_{\rho}\} is omitted for an unlocalized target. These associations connect the requested target and newly localized participants to the human whose interaction prompted the observation, forming candidate pairs for grounded relation verification.

A.3 Relation-Agnostic Geometric Adjudication

One grounding per identity.

For an identity with multiple grounding candidates, the MLLM compares their category and box descriptions against the full image and acquired crops. Each candidate is assigned an answer letter, and the candidate with the highest answer support is selected. The judgment considers the participant’s identity, category, and complete visible extent to establish a shared grounding across actions and roles. Identities with one candidate retain their original grounding.

The selected geometry is shared by every relation involving the participant: for relations d1d_{1} and d2d_{2} containing identity ii, bi​(d1)=bi​(d2)=bi∗b_{i}(d_{1})=b_{i}(d_{2})=b_{i}^{*}, where bi∗=bi,mi∗b_{i}^{*}=b_{i,m_{i}^{*}}. With at most two observations, an identity has at most three candidates: its initial or discovery grounding and up to two local revisions.

A.4 Grounded Interaction Reasoning

Question construction.

The question context comprises the selected participants’ identities, categories, and image-coordinate boxes, the public action or role definition, and the corresponding image views. Pair questions assess the presence of an interaction, and action questions verify a specific predicate. Agent, role-state, and binding questions respectively assess action occurrence, target visibility, and role identity. The prompt formulations appear in Appendix G.

Visual context.

Localization and discovery use the full image, local observation uses the requested crop, and geometric adjudication receives all acquired views. Relation questions use the full image and, when available, one local view associated with the queried participants. The source view vi,mi∗v_{i,m_{i}^{*}} of a selected grounding takes priority, with the most recent observation chosen when both participants have local source views. If neither selected grounding has a local source view, the crop is taken from the most recent compatible observation request.

A compatible request concerns the same human and agrees with the question’s specified action and target, or leaves those attributes unspecified. For role questions, it concerns the queried role or general participant localization. Agent questions admit requests for any role, pair questions use general participant requests, and no-interaction questions impose no action or role restriction. The full image provides the visual context when no compatible local view is available.

Answer support.

Answer supports are obtained by normalizing the raw first-token logits according to Equation 2. Pair, action, agent, and binding questions use {false, true, unknown}; role-state questions use {missing, visible, unknown}; geometry questions use the candidate letters. Each label corresponds to one token. These normalized supports determine the selected geometry and final detection scores, with the generation temperature applied to perceptual generation alone.

Candidate retention and multi-label prediction.

Discovery and observation associations complement visual pair assessment in Equation 4, with 𝒫D∪𝒫O⊆𝒦\mathcal{P}_{D}\cup\mathcal{P}_{O}\subseteq\mathcal{K}. Each retained HICO-DET pair is evaluated over all positive actions compatible with its target category, using a separate answer distribution for each action. The no_interaction label is evaluated independently over all directed pairs.

Physical and missing role targets.

V-COCO uses the agent support qAq_{A}, role-state supports qVq_{V} and qMq_{M}, and binding support qBq_{B} defined in the main text. Physical candidates share the action and visibility factors and receive individual binding assessments, giving sphysical=qA​qV​qBs_{\mathrm{physical}}=q_{A}q_{V}q_{B}. The NULL alternative combines action and missing-target support as sNULL=qA​qMs_{\mathrm{NULL}}=q_{A}q_{M}. Since visible, missing, and unknown states share one answer distribution, qV+qM≤1q_{V}+q_{M}\leq 1; the combined score of any one physical candidate and its NULL alternative is bounded by qAq_{A}.

A.5 Complete Inference Procedure

Table 6 summarizes the complete inference procedure, from participant localization and observation to grounded interaction prediction.

Appendix B Experimental Setup and Evaluation Protocols

B.1 Detection and Semantic-Role Evaluation

HICO-DET.

We evaluate all 9,658 official test images over 600 human-object interaction classes, comprising 520 positive-interaction classes and 80 no_interaction classes. Each prediction consists of a human box, an object box, an interaction class, and a confidence score. A detection is correct when its class matches the annotation and both boxes reach IoU 0.5. Predictions are matched in descending score order within each class, with at most one true positive per annotation. Rare contains 138 classes with fewer than ten training instances, and Non-Rare contains the remaining 462 classes.

Default evaluation includes all test images. Known Object evaluates each interaction class on images containing an annotated instance of its object category. Both settings use the same predictions, with Known Object restricting the images considered when assessing false positives.

Average precision.

HICO-DET uses the VOC 2007 eleven-point definition (Everingham et al., 2010). For class cc, let pc​(r)p_{c}(r) denote precision at an attained recall value rr, and let ℛAP={0,0.1,…,1}\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{AP}}=\{0,0.1,\ldots,1\}. Then

APc=111​∑t∈ℛAPmaxr≥t⁡pc​(r),mAP⁡(𝒞)=1|𝒞|​∑c∈𝒞APc,\mathrm{AP}_{c}=\frac{1}{11}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{AP}}}\max_{r\geq t}p_{c}(r),\qquad\mathrm{mAP}(\mathcal{C})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\mathrm{AP}_{c}, (11)

where a recall threshold with no qualifying prediction contributes zero. Full mAP averages all 600 classes. We report AP as percentages and compute differences before rounding.

V-COCO.

We evaluate all 4,946 official test images. Agent evaluation measures whether the localized person performs one of 26 actions. Role evaluation additionally identifies the target fulfilling the corresponding semantic role and averages over 25 action-role categories, including point. Actions such as hit, eat, and cut distinguish an object from an instrument. Conversely, stand, walk, run, and smile have agent annotations without a target role.

For a role with an annotated physical target, both the person and role target must match at IoU 0.5. When the role target is annotated as missing, Scenario 1 (S1) requires a matching person and a NULL target prediction. Scenario 2 (S2) relaxes target localization for that missing-role annotation. Both scenarios follow the benchmark’s treatment of incompletely annotated people and integrate the precision-recall envelope.

V-COCO reporting conventions.

The primary S1/S2 metric for HarnessHOI, direct-generation baselines, and ablations is the 25-role mean, including point. Appendix C.5 additionally gives the 24-role mean excluding point and the 26-action agent mean. Published comparison results retain their sources’ role definitions and missing-target conventions; the S1/S2 columns follow the scenario designations in those sources.

Coordinate conventions.

Predicted boxes use coordinates normalized within the input view and are mapped to image pixels for evaluation. HICO-DET then shifts all four zero-based coordinates by one and computes IoU with inclusive pixel extents, following its annotation convention. Crop coordinates are mapped to the full image as specified in Appendix A. All official test images are evaluated, including empty outputs and valid detections from partially completed inference.

B.2 Class Partitions and Development Settings

Open-vocabulary partitions.

We report rare-first unseen combinations (RF-UC), non-rare-first unseen combinations (NF-UC), unseen objects (UO), and unseen verbs (UV). The Unseen subsets contain 120, 120, 100, and 84 classes, respectively; their Seen complements contain 480, 480, 500, and 516 classes. We use the class masks released with GEN-VLKT (Liao et al., 2022). Each partition aggregates the same class AP values from the same predictions. In particular,

mAPFull=|𝒞U|​mAPU+|𝒞S|​mAPS600,\mathrm{mAP}_{\mathrm{Full}}=\frac{|\mathcal{C}_{U}|\mathrm{mAP}_{U}+|\mathcal{C}_{S}|\mathrm{mAP}_{S}}{600}, (12)

where 𝒞U\mathcal{C}_{U} and 𝒞S\mathcal{C}_{S} are the benchmark’s Unseen and Seen class sets. HarnessHOI uses the full public interaction vocabulary and the same frozen model and inference policy across these partitions. The class masks are applied to the resulting AP values, so the Full result is shared by all four settings.

Development protocol.

Prompts and inference policy are developed using evaluation feedback from fixed subsets of the official train set: 128 images for optimization and 256 for confirmation, with four additional images for interface checks. Development feedback also includes train-image inspection and evaluation on the complete train set. The final configuration is evaluated on every image in the official test sets.

The optimization and confirmation sets are sampled without replacement from disjoint source subsets, excluding the interface images. Sampling uses fixed seeds, and each image retains its index in the official train list for generation across both development-subset and complete-train-set runs. The image lists and seed assignments will accompany the released evaluation configurations.

Model inputs.

The model remains frozen throughout development and evaluation. Its inference inputs comprise the image, generated participants, and public action and role definitions. Target-benchmark annotations are used for development feedback, evaluation, and the ground-truth-based analyses described below; they are not supplied to the model at inference.

B.3 Model and Inference Configuration

We use frozen Qwen3.5-9B for participant localization, interaction discovery, local observation, and grounded question answering. Its native visual encoder processes both the full image and local crops. Table 7 summarizes the inference settings.

Image views.

The image processor preserves aspect ratio and aligns the input dimensions to the model’s visual grid. Local crops are extracted from the original image and encoded by the same backbone.

Generation and scoring.

Perceptual generation produces participants, interaction hypotheses, and localization updates. Visual question answering uses one output token with decoding temperature zero; answer support is computed from the raw logits before output-grammar modification. Independent generation runs preserve the image and stage seed offsets and vary the base seed as specified in Appendix E.5.

Detection output.

We retain continuous detection scores and merge exact duplicate predictions by maximum support. No score threshold or non-maximum suppression is applied. V-COCO predictions include agent actions, physical-role targets, and NULL alternatives, scored according to Equation 8.

B.4 Baseline Inference

We compare three inference strategies using frozen Qwen3.5-9B on the complete test sets. Direct generation predicts participants and relations in one response, with a shared person box across actions. The initial-instance baseline applies visual pair assessment and relation verification to the initially localized participants. HarnessHOI additionally performs interaction-guided discovery, observation, and geometric adjudication. Direct generation uses the same full-image processing, sampling settings, and initial output budget.

Direct-generation confidence.

For each generated interaction record, let 𝒥\mathcal{J} contain the token positions overlapping its emitted interaction label. The direct-generation score is the geometric mean of the corresponding token probabilities:

sgen=exp⁡(1|𝒥|​∑j∈𝒥log⁡pθ​(yj∣I,y<j)).s_{\mathrm{gen}}=\exp\!\left(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{J}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\log p_{\theta}(y_{j}\mid I,y_{<j})\right). (13)

We use token probabilities before output-grammar modification. HICO-DET scores the emitted verb-object label; V-COCO scores the action label and assigns this score to its agent prediction and explicitly generated physical or NULL roles.

B.5 Evaluation Coverage

Evaluation includes all 9,658 HICO-DET and 4,946 V-COCO test images. Valid predictions from partially completed inference are evaluated normally. Images with no predictions, numbering 98 and 12 on the two benchmarks, respectively, remain in the evaluation population.

B.6 Evaluation Implementations

We use a common evaluator for HarnessHOI, its ablations, and the released predictions re-evaluated in Tables 13 and 14. Tables 8 and 9 compare this implementation with the original HICO-DET code under Octave and the original V-COCO evaluator on the same predictions, including direct generation and the principal perceptual and relational ablations.

On HICO-DET, the original code under Octave gives 32.97% Default and 36.61% Known Object Full mAP, compared with 33.20% and 36.85% from the common evaluator. The difference follows from the recall-threshold sequences constructed by the two implementations, which sample the precision envelope at slightly different boundaries in eleven-point AP. V-COCO role scores agree at the reported precision.

Appendix C Extended Benchmark Results

C.1 Regular and Open-Vocabulary Comparisons

Tables 10 and 11 provide the complete regular and open-vocabulary comparisons corresponding to Tables 1 and 2. They include additional backbone configurations, MLLM-based methods, retrieval baselines, and the training-free variant of DA-HOI.

DA-HOI and vision-language baselines.

The fine-tuned DA-HOI (Xuan et al., 2026) comparisons include both DETR and GroundingDINO configurations under regular and open-vocabulary evaluation. Its training-free variant combines R50-DETR proposals with deterministic MLLM generation. DYSCO (Tonini et al., 2025) uses LongCLIP-L for regular evaluation and CLIP ViT-B/16 for open-vocabulary evaluation.

Other comparison configurations.

GEN-VLKT uses its large and small configurations for regular and open-vocabulary evaluation, respectively. VDRP follows its default ViT-B configuration for regular evaluation and its ViT-L configuration for open-vocabulary evaluation. The UO result of EZ-HOI uses its HICO-DET-pretrained detector. The CLIP baseline follows LAIN (Kim et al., 2025); direct Qwen inference and LongCLIP retrieval follow HOI-R1 and DYSCO. LINK’s V-COCO S2 result follows its ICLR version. V-COCO reporting conventions are specified in Appendix B.1.

C.2 Models and Inference Resources

Table 12 compares the models, inference strategies, and additional resources used by related methods. HarnessHOI uses one frozen MLLM for participant acquisition, geometric adjudication, and relation verification. The public vocabulary and development protocol are specified in Appendix B.

Agent-based HOI inference.

AgentHOI by Wang et al. (Wang et al., 2026) combines hypothesis proposal with multi-agent debate, whereas AgentHOI by Lei et al. (Lei et al., 2026) combines multi-round interaction reasoning with instance-specific visual grounding. Table 10 includes both methods under regular evaluation, while Table 11 includes the open-vocabulary results reported by Lei et al. Wang et al. also report 14.58 mAP on V-COCO without an S1/S2 designation.

Task-optimized configurations.

The extended tables include the learned interaction representations of FineHOI (Tonini et al., 2026), SGC-Net (Lin et al., 2025), Funnel-HOI (Sarma et al., 2026), ScriptHOI (Nguyen et al., 2026), and HOIBlender (Chen and Yanai, 2026), with their reported backbone configurations. UniHOI by Yang et al. (Yang et al., 2026) jointly learns detection and generation in a unified token space; UniHOI-s (Cao et al., 2023) denotes the earlier BLIP-2-based detector. Table 10 also includes the three SFT+GRPO backbones reported by HOI-R1 (Chen et al., 2025). MLLM distillation in CL-HOI (Gao et al., 2025) and generative evaluation in HOI-MLLM (Wu et al., 2026b) are presented with their respective metrics in Appendix C.6.

Tool-augmented interaction reasoning.

ImagineAgent (Yuan et al., 2026) learns interaction reasoning through supervised fine-tuning and tool-augmented reinforcement learning, combining image cropping, retrieval, and generative modeling to augment its observations. Related visual-agent work learns to select heterogeneous visual experts across reasoning rounds (Fan et al., 2026). HarnessHOI uses the same frozen MLLM for visual exploration and relation verification, with geometric adjudication establishing the participant groundings shared across actions and roles.

C.3 Common-Evaluator Comparison

Tables 13 and 14 evaluate the released predictions of AgentHOI by Lei et al. and HarnessHOI with identical matching and AP computation, complementing the source-reported comparisons above.

We evaluate the released AgentHOI (Lei et al., 2026) predictions with the authors’ default score completion, sigmoid, box exponent 0.3, and threshold 0.1.11 1 AgentHOI release identifier: 5599af3794f6b6006be156da353e54f9ca64f486. The release covers 9,546 test images, including 23 without boxes. The remaining 112 official test images receive empty predictions. Both methods are evaluated over the complete test set using identical inclusive-IoU, matching, and sorting conventions.

HarnessHOI consistently outperforms AgentHOI under the same evaluator, with improvements on both Rare and Non-Rare classes under Default and Known Object evaluation. The gains also extend to Unseen classes in all four open-vocabulary settings (Table 14).

C.4 HICO-DET Interaction Classes

Positive interactions and no interaction.

Table 15 reports results for the 520 positive-interaction and 80 no-interaction classes. Default mAP is 36.84% and 9.55%, respectively, giving a class-weighted Full mAP of 33.20%. The corresponding Known Object results are 39.79% and 17.73%. Positive actions and no-interaction labels are assessed through separate visual questions.

Frequency and evaluation domain.

Rare and Non-Rare mAP average the classes within each frequency group, whereas coverage and true-positive counts aggregate individual annotations. Default and Known Object evaluation yield the same 22,161 true positives. Their AP differs because Known Object restricts the images considered for each class and therefore changes the false-positive distribution.

C.5 V-COCO Actions and Semantic Roles

Table 16 reports S1/S2 AP and matching statistics for all 25 roles. Of the 12,423 physical-role and 3,969 missing-role annotations, the predictions match 9,728 and 3,854, respectively. S1 and S2 produce the same final true-positive counts in these results, while their missing-role criteria change the matching order and precision-recall curves. S2 exceeds S1 for every role, with small gaps for roles with few missing annotations such as surf, skateboard, and drink, and large gaps for roles with many missing annotations such as lay and eat/instr. The corresponding 24-role means, excluding point, are 46.09% and 51.07%; the 26-action agent mean is 75.58%.

Agent-level action recognition.

Table 17 reports all 26 agent actions, including the four without target roles. HarnessHOI obtains 75.58% mean agent AP by assessing each action on the localized person. For role-bearing actions, the same support is combined with target visibility and binding to produce role predictions.

C.6 Results under Related Evaluation Protocols

We summarize related results on MLLM distillation, generative HOI prediction, and instruction-conditioned detection under their respective evaluation protocols.

Cross-level distillation results.

Table 18 presents CL-HOI under full supervision and MLLM distillation, including its ResNet-50 and Swin-L configurations. The reported metrics are HICO-DET Full mAP and the authors’ V-COCO Role AP. The distillation setting transfers image-level interaction knowledge from the MLLM to an instance-level detector.

Generative interaction results.

Table 19 reports HOI-MLLM with Qwen2.5-VL-3B using mean F1, precision, and recall. Its end-to-end configuration jointly predicts participants and interactions, the R50-DETR configuration supplies predicted object boxes, and Oracle supplies ground-truth boxes. These settings examine interaction reasoning with different sources of participant localization.

Instruction-conditioned detection.

HOID-R1 by Zhang et al. (Zhang et al., 2025b) evaluates fine-grained, precise, and open-vocabulary instructions on a reannotated HICO-DET benchmark (Table 20). Its Seen and Unseen groups refer to image subsets. Human and object mIoU, action accuracy, and mAP measure localization and interaction recognition under these instruction settings.

Appendix D Harness Design Analysis

We examine how interaction-guided perception, geometric adjudication, and grounded interaction reasoning contribute to HOI detection. Table 21 summarizes the experimental conditions used to evaluate each component.

D.1 Effectiveness of the Complete Harness

Table 3 compares direct generation, the initial-instance baseline, and the complete harness under the scoring rules in Appendix B.4. Grounded verification over the initial participants substantially improves detection over direct generation. Interaction-guided perception and geometric adjudication further improve results on both benchmarks.

D.2 Complete Ablation Results

Tables 22 and 23 report the complete HICO-DET and V-COCO metrics for the ablations examined in this section.

Table 24 reports the complete ablations under RF-UC, NF-UC, UO, and UV. Each variant is evaluated across the four class partitions using its predictions from regular evaluation. HarnessHOI obtains Unseen mAP of 40.15%, 33.64%, 35.45%, and 33.87%, respectively. Its advantage over direct generation extends across combinations, object categories, and actions. The pair and label ablations examine the contribution of candidate selection and compatible-action verification within these class groups.

D.3 Interaction-Guided Perception

Interaction-guided perception uses action and role hypotheses to discover relevant participants and select regions for closer observation. We first evaluate participant discovery and local observation, then compare them with repeated localization and non-directed observation to examine the contribution of interaction guidance.

Participant discovery and targeted observation.

The discovered-participant ablation excludes identities introduced by discovery and performs observation and relation assessment over the remaining participants. The observation ablation retains global discovery and its single localization per instance, omitting local observation and the corresponding geometric adjudication. These component configurations are reported in Table 3, with full metrics in Tables 22 and 23.

Guidance for participant discovery.

The repeated-localization control receives the same full image, initial participant identities, and designated human groups as interaction-guided discovery. Its question directly requests additional visible participants associated with those humans. Both conditions use the same generation budget and the observation requests produced by interaction-guided discovery, followed by the same observation, geometric adjudication, and relation verification. Interaction-guided discovery improves detection on both benchmarks (Table 4), supporting the use of interaction semantics to direct participant search.

Selection of local observations.

To evaluate region selection, the non-directed control retains the discovery output, target descriptions, observation count, and crop dimensions. Each crop center is sampled uniformly from valid image positions using a fixed seed. Both conditions use the same image processing and localization instructions, followed by geometric and relational assessment on their acquired observations. The gains from targeted observation in Table 4 demonstrate the value of selecting regions according to the interaction hypothesis.

Stage-wise participant coverage.

We measure grounding coverage and relation-candidate coverage to evaluate participant acquisition at successive stages. Grounding coverage requires participant boxes that match an annotation at IoU 0.5, while candidate coverage additionally requires the corresponding action or role label. Each annotation is counted once.

Initial localization and discovery are evaluated on their respective participant sets. The all-localization condition uses the accumulated grounding candidates, and the selected-grounding condition uses one adjudicated candidate per identity. Physical interactions require matching human and target instances with distinct identities; HICO-DET also requires the target category to match. Missing roles require a matching person, together with the appropriate NULL prediction for candidate coverage.

As shown in Table 25, discovery adds matching groundings for 571 HICO-DET interactions and 217 V-COCO roles. Local observation extends coverage by a further 12 and 23 annotations, respectively. The final selected groundings cover 22,895 HICO-DET interactions and 14,473 V-COCO roles, providing the participant pairs for subsequent verification.

Interaction configurations.

We group the interaction annotations by participant and action structure. The multiple-human-box group contains images with at least two distinct annotated human boxes. The HICO-DET multiple-target group contains annotations whose action has at least two distinct physical targets within the image. For V-COCO, the corresponding multiple-target-state group treats each distinct physical target and NULL as target states, while reporting physical-role annotations. Small targets occupy at most 1% of the image area. The multiple-action group contains human-target pairs annotated with at least two actions, including NULL targets in V-COCO. Groups may overlap, and their sizes count annotations.

Missing-role annotations form a separate V-COCO group and contribute to the full totals. Their grounding and candidate coverage follow the person and NULL criteria above. The small-target group includes physical targets alone.

Coverage in complex scenes.

The full harness covers 878 additional HICO-DET interactions and 925 additional V-COCO roles over the initial-instance baseline (Table 26 and Figure 4). These gains include 172 and 447 annotations with small targets, respectively, and 534 V-COCO roles involving multiple actions. Table 27 reports the corresponding stage-wise coverage. For V-COCO small targets, coverage increases from 3,407 after initial localization to 3,518 after discovery and 3,529 after observation, with 3,208 annotations represented in the final relation candidates.

The gains on small targets demonstrate the effectiveness of interaction-guided perception in recovering visually inconspicuous participants. Improvements on multiple-action pairs further show that the acquired groundings support several interactions involving the same entities.

D.4 Relation-Agnostic Geometric Adjudication

We evaluate geometric adjudication by retaining discovery and observation and replacing visual selection with the first box associated with each identity (Table 3). This comparison examines the contribution of selecting a shared participant grounding from the acquired localization candidates.

On HICO-DET and V-COCO, 479 and 424 identities adopt an observation-derived grounding, respectively. The selected grounding is shared across all relations involving the participant. The improvement over first-candidate geometry in Table 3 confirms the effectiveness of visual adjudication for interaction grounding.

Criterion for shared grounding.

Relation-conditioned and relation-agnostic adjudication receive identical candidate boxes and image views for each instance. Relation-conditioned adjudication adds the earliest discovery or observation association involving that instance and asks which candidate best localizes the participant in that interaction. Relation-agnostic adjudication uses the identity, category, and visible extent criterion in Section 3.3. Instances without a recorded association use the common identity-based criterion. Both conditions select one shared grounding per instance and apply the same subsequent relation verification.

With candidate boxes and image views fixed, relation-agnostic adjudication improves detection on both benchmarks (Table 4). The results support selecting shared groundings according to participant identity, category, and visible extent, independently of the proposed relation.

D.5 Grounded Interaction Reasoning

We examine grounded interaction reasoning through complementary pair selection, multi-label verification, and compositional semantic-role assessment. These comparisons evaluate which participant pairs and relations are considered and how their visual evidence determines the final predictions.

Context for relation verification.

The proposal-conditioned control appends the original discovery proposals associated with the queried participants to the final action, agent, role-state, and binding questions. The harness condition uses the selected participants, public relation definitions, and image evidence. Pair retention, candidate relations, boxes, views, answer labels, and score composition are identical. Both conditions assess the full candidate domain, including relations absent from the discovery proposals. Grounded verification improves detection over proposal-conditioned questions on these identical candidates (Table 4), demonstrating the benefit of assessing relations directly from the acquired visual evidence.

Complementary relation candidates.

Table 28(a) compares visual pair assessment, discovery and observation associations 𝒫D∪𝒫O\mathcal{P}_{D}\cup\mathcal{P}_{O}, and their union 𝒦\mathcal{K}. Each configuration retains the original relation scores on its selected pairs, together with HICO-DET no-interaction and V-COCO agent and NULL predictions. Combining the two sources achieves the best results on both benchmarks, improving HICO-DET mAP by 5.11 points over discovery and observation associations and V-COCO AP by 1.42/1.93 points over visual pair assessment. The gains demonstrate that associations established during perception complement the relations identified by visual pair assessment.

Coverage and selective verification.

The final candidates cover 22,232 HICO-DET interactions and 13,628 V-COCO roles, retaining 97.1% and 94.2% of the annotations covered by the selected groundings. Positive-action and role-binding verification uses 39,791 of 416,280 human-entity pairs on HICO-DET and 17,804 of 251,376 on V-COCO. Thus, pair selection reduces the respective domains by 90.4% and 92.9% while retaining high coverage of the grounded interactions.

Coverage measures the existence of matching candidates. Detection evaluation additionally assigns each prediction to its best-matching annotation and removes duplicates in score order. A prediction overlapping several annotations contributes at most one true positive, so final matching counts can differ from candidate coverage. The ranking bounds in Appendix E.4 follow the evaluator’s assignment rule.

Multi-label interaction verification.

We evaluate label expansion on the pairs represented by explicitly proposed and scored relations, denoted by 𝒫prop\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{prop}}. The proposed-label condition retains these relations; the compatible-label condition includes all assessed category-compatible positive actions in HICO-DET or all 25 action-role categories in V-COCO on the same pairs. An observation association enters 𝒫O\mathcal{P}_{O}, whereas membership in 𝒫prop\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{prop}} requires a scored relation proposal. Geometry, image evidence, scores, and all no-interaction, agent, and NULL predictions remain fixed.

As shown in Table 28(b), label expansion increases HICO-DET mAP from 18.35% to 29.85% and V-COCO AP from 36.43%/39.81% to 42.27%/47.14%. The gains demonstrate the importance of verifying multiple compatible relations over shared participants, extending prediction beyond the labels proposed during discovery.

Answer support and role factors.

Role visibility and binding are assessed conditionally on the action, while qAq_{A} supplies the evidence that the person performs it. For a given person, action, and role, physical candidates share qA​qVq_{A}q_{V} and are ordered by their binding support qBq_{B}. Across people and images, action and visibility also contribute to the confidence ranking used for role AP. Table 23 examines these factors and the treatment of unresolved and missing targets.

The binary-readout ablation removes unknown support and renormalizes false/true or missing/visible within each final question, preserving pair retention and score composition. The action-factor ablation uses qV​qBq_{V}q_{B} for physical targets and qMq_{M} for NULL targets. The visibility-factor ablation uses qA​qBq_{A}q_{B} for physical targets and preserves NULL scores. Both retain the original agent predictions. The NULL ablation removes missing-target predictions while retaining physical-role and agent outputs. All four conditions are derived from the full method’s answer supports.

Compositional role verification.

We compare compositional verification with a joint action-and-role question on identical participants, geometry, and role candidates. Each physical-target joint question uses the same full-image and crop inputs as its corresponding binding question; each NULL joint question uses those of its corresponding role-state question. The joint question evaluates action occurrence together with the target’s role; its NULL formulation evaluates action occurrence together with the absence of a visible role target. True-label support directly scores each candidate, with agent predictions unchanged.

Compositional verification improves V-COCO S1/S2 AP from 41.10%/46.30% to 44.65%/49.70% (Table 28(c)), with gains on 15 of 25 roles in S1 and 20 of 25 in S2. The final true-positive counts remain unchanged, showing that the improvement comes from more accurate ranking of role predictions. Image-paired bootstrap with 1,000 resamples gives 95% percentile intervals of [3.02, 4.10] and [2.85, 3.96] points for the S1 and S2 gains.

Role-specific confidence composition.

Table 29 and Figure 5 report the comparison for all 25 roles. Compositional verification improves both roles of hit and the instrument role of cut under S1 and S2, with a 26.29-point gain for eat/instr under S1. The gains demonstrate the effectiveness of combining shared action evidence with the visibility and binding evidence of each role target.

Image-paired resampling.

For the joint and compositional role comparison, we draw 1,000 paired bootstrap samples of the test images with replacement (Efron, 1979), using seed 20260920. Each sample contains the original number of images and assigns identical image multiplicities to both methods’ predictions and annotations. We recompute AP under the original matching rules and class denominator, assigning zero to classes absent from a sample. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the paired AP differences form the confidence interval for each scenario.

Missing role targets.

Explicit missing-role assessment represents actions whose targets are not visible in the image. Removing NULL predictions reduces S1 AP from 44.65% to 39.20%, while the complete method obtains 49.70% under S2 (Table 23). This comparison demonstrates the importance of distinguishing a missing role target from an absent action.

D.6 Backbone Generality

We apply the identical harness configuration, public vocabulary, and evaluator to Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025) and InternVL3-8B (Zhu et al., 2025) on the complete test sets under generation seed 66. Table 30 reports the complete-harness results for each backbone.

InternVL3-8B obtains 32.11% HICO-DET Full mAP and 43.60%/48.40% V-COCO S1/S2 AP, while Qwen2.5-VL-7B obtains 31.61% and 43.10%/47.90%, respectively. The same three-stage harness supports action-triplet and semantic-role prediction across these backbones, demonstrating its applicability to different MLLMs.

Appendix E Inference Computation and Stability

We analyze the computational cost and generation stability of HarnessHOI. Comparisons with repeated direct generation examine the benefit of coordinating perception and reasoning, while ground-truth-assisted ranking separates candidate quality from confidence estimation.

E.1 Computational Structure

Perceptual generation comprises participant localization, interaction discovery, and local observation. Discovery groups share the initially localized participants and can be processed concurrently. Let H0H_{0} be the number of initially localized humans and RR the number of local observations. With four humans per discovery group, the number of generative responses is

Ngen=1+⌈H04⌉+R,0≤R≤2.N_{\mathrm{gen}}=1+\left\lceil\frac{H_{0}}{4}\right\rceil+R,\qquad 0\leq R\leq 2. (14)

For CC distinct crop windows, the visual context comprises 1+C1+C views, with C≤RC\leq R. Their encoded representations are shared across the associated generation and verification requests.

Candidate verification evaluates independent questions through first-token answer scores. Geometric adjudication selects the participant groundings used in pair assessment and action or role verification. Independent questions within each stage are processed with continuous batching. Let H=|ℋ∗|H=|\mathcal{H}^{*}|, N=|ℰ∗|N=|\mathcal{E}^{*}|, P=H⁡(N−1)P=H(N-1), K=|𝒦|K=|\mathcal{K}|, and let GG count identities with multiple geometry candidates. The number of scoring requests on HICO-DET is

NscoreHICO=G+2​P+∑(h,o)∈𝒦|𝒜+​(co∗)|.N_{\mathrm{score}}^{\mathrm{HICO}}=G+2P+\sum_{(h,o)\in\mathcal{K}}|\mathcal{A}^{+}(c_{o}^{*})|. (15)

The two pair terms correspond to interaction assessment and no-interaction assessment. Positive-action verification covers the category-compatible actions of each retained pair. On V-COCO, the scoring workload is

NscoreVCOCO=G+51​H+P+25​K.N_{\mathrm{score}}^{\mathrm{VCOCO}}=G+51H+P+25K. (16)

Agent-action and role-state assessment contribute 26​H26H and 25​H25H requests, respectively; each retained pair contributes 25 role-binding requests. In both benchmarks, the verification workload depends on the number of grounded participants and retained relation candidates.

E.2 Measured Computation

Table 31 reports the per-image computation and hardware cost of the harness. Perceptual generation requires an average of 2.51 and 2.78 responses per image on HICO-DET and V-COCO, respectively, with a median of two on both benchmarks. Candidate verification processes independent scoring questions in batches. Table 32 reports their mean, median, and 95th percentile for each type of question, reflecting the variation in candidate-set size across images.

Hardware cost.

Hardware cost is measured independently as amortized GPU-worker time, computed by summing the recorded processing time across GPU workers and dividing by the number of images. The measurement includes input preparation, model inference, and result collection, with all recorded inference work counted once; model loading and evaluation are excluded. On HICO-DET and V-COCO, the measured costs are 13.26 and 22.07 GPU-worker seconds per image, respectively.

Execution settings.

Hardware measurements use frozen Qwen3.5-9B in BF16 on NVIDIA A6000 GPUs, with one model replica per GPU, four active images per replica, and up to 32 concurrent requests per GPU. The harness measurement uses four GPUs. Continuous batching schedules generation and scoring requests, while shared visual representations and prefix caching reuse the common image and prompt context. The cache hit rates in Table 31 measure the fraction of scoring input tokens served from the prefix cache.

Ablation computation.

Pair, label, and factor ablations use the same relation supports to evaluate alternative candidate sets and score compositions. The V-COCO joint action-and-role control evaluates new questions with the view assignment specified in Appendix D.5. Perceptual ablations use the participants and views produced by each configuration. Shared computations are counted once when measuring a complete inference configuration.

E.3 Allocating Inference Computation

We compare the harness with repeated direct generation to examine how coordinated perception and reasoning affect detection performance and computational cost. Both methods use the same frozen backbone, full-image processing, sampling settings, and initial output budget. Repeated generation independently predicts participants and relations in each response, whereas the harness uses interaction hypotheses to acquire visual evidence for grounded verification.

Repeated generation and fusion.

We combine the first K∈{1,2,4,8}K\in\{1,2,4,8\} responses in a predetermined order using two fusion rules. Exact-match fusion retains the maximum score among predictions with identical categories, roles, target states, and boxes. Pair-IoU suppression removes lower-scored duplicates at threshold 0.5 within the same category, role, and target state. The hardware cost at each KK sums the recorded GPU-worker processing time of the constituent generation runs per image. Tables 33 and 34 report both rules on the same response sets.

Performance and computation.

Figure 6 presents detection performance alongside hardware cost. With pair-IoU suppression, increasing the number of responses from one to eight raises HICO-DET mAP from 15.61% to 19.84% and V-COCO AP from 16.38%/21.18% to 22.21%/26.50%. The measured eight-response costs are 19.95 and 20.94 GPU-worker seconds per image, respectively. HarnessHOI achieves 33.20% and 44.65%/49.70%, with measured costs of 13.26 and 22.07 seconds per image. The gains over repeated generation demonstrate the effectiveness of coordinating visual exploration and relation verification within the harness.

Fusion and candidate construction.

Repeated sampling produces additional interaction candidates and overlapping detections with slightly different boxes. Exact-match fusion retains these duplicates, and AP decreases as more responses are combined. Pair-IoU suppression improves AP by removing overlapping detections from the same responses. The following analysis evaluates candidate quality through the best AP attainable by reordering the predicted boxes and labels.

E.4 Fixed-Candidate Ranking Analysis

We evaluate the quality of the generated candidates by fixing their boxes and labels and using ground-truth annotations to determine the optimal ranking.

Single-response candidates.

Table 35 compares the harness with ground-truth-assisted ranking of a single direct-generation response. The resulting ranking upper bounds are 21.58% HICO-DET mAP and 30.69%/35.01% V-COCO AP. HarnessHOI exceeds these bounds by 11.62 and 13.96/14.69 points, respectively, demonstrating that its advantage extends beyond confidence estimation to the participants and relations available for prediction.

Interaction candidates beyond repeated generation.

With eight responses, exact-match fusion reaches ranking upper bounds of 30.50% HICO-DET mAP and 41.90%/46.40% V-COCO AP. HarnessHOI exceeds these bounds with its predicted scores by 2.70 and 2.75/3.30 points, respectively, and also exceeds the pair-IoU bounds of 30.09% and 41.40%/45.90%. The advantage persists even when the repeated-generation predictions are ranked optimally, demonstrating the importance of interaction-guided participant discovery and relation construction for HOI detection.

Ground-truth ranking.

For each response count and fusion rule, we compute the maximum AP obtainable by reordering the fixed predictions. Ground-truth matching identifies one correct prediction per covered annotation and ranks these predictions before false positives. Boxes, labels, and candidate counts remain unchanged, and HICO-DET averages over all 600 classes.

Ranking bound under fixed matching.

The evaluators assign each prediction to its best-matching ground-truth instance before duplicate assignment: HICO-DET uses participant-pair overlap, while V-COCO first selects the best-matching person and then assesses its role target. A duplicate does not switch to a second-best annotation. For fixed predicted boxes and labels, the set of annotations with an eligible matching prediction is therefore fixed. Let McM_{c} be the number of such annotations for class cc and Gc>0G_{c}>0 its ground-truth count. Placing one eligible prediction for each of these annotations before false positives attains precision one up to recall Mc/GcM_{c}/G_{c}. Under the respective AP definitions, the class-wise bounds are

UcHICO\displaystyle U_{c}^{\mathrm{HICO}} =𝟏[Mc>0]11∑t∈ℛAP[t≤McGc],\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbf{1}[M_{c}>0]}{11}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{AP}}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[t\leq\frac{M_{c}}{G_{c}}\right], (17)
UcVCOCO\displaystyle U_{c}^{\mathrm{VCOCO}} =McGc.\displaystyle=\frac{M_{c}}{G_{c}}.

Here ℛAP\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{AP}} is the HICO-DET evaluator’s recall-threshold sequence. V-COCO uses the matching rule of each role scenario, with S1 and S2 ranked separately. Averaging the class-wise bounds gives the results in Tables 35 and 36.

E.5 Generation Stability

We evaluate each method with generation seeds 66, 67, and 68, keeping the backbone, inference policy, and complete test set fixed. For the harness, the seed controls participant localization, discovery, and observation, while grounded verification uses the same first-token scoring rule. Table 37 reports the individual runs, and Table 38 gives the HICO-DET results under Default, Known Object, Rare, and Non-Rare evaluation.

Stability across benchmarks.

Across three HICO-DET runs, HarnessHOI obtains 32.95% mean Default Full mAP with a sample standard deviation of 0.22 points, compared with 15.66% ±\pm 0.13 for direct generation. Its Default Rare and Non-Rare means are 41.28% and 30.46%, and its Known Object Full mean is 36.58%. The gains remain consistent across seeds, evaluation settings, and frequency groups. V-COCO exhibits the same advantage in all three runs under both role-evaluation scenarios (Table 37).

Appendix F Qualitative Results

Figure 8 illustrates how the harness coordinates participant discovery, targeted observation, and grounded reasoning. Interaction hypotheses guide the recovery of the book and shared bench. The recovered book supports both hold and read, and a common bench grounding supports the sitting relations of two people. In the tennis scene, the racket participates in both hold and hit, while role verification distinguishes the racket as the instrument and the ball as the object of hitting. These examples complement the coverage analysis in Appendix D.3 by showing how the acquired participants support multiple actions and semantic roles.

Figures 9, 10, and 11 provide detailed examples of participant recovery, pair selection, and semantic-role assignment, with the corresponding visual-question scores reported below.

F.1 Participant Discovery and Targeted Observation

Recovering a book.

In HICO-DET image 00000116, interaction discovery recovers a book omitted from initial localization and associates it with the person’s holding and reading actions. The two actions are then verified independently using the same person-book groundings. Table 39 reports the localization overlaps and relation scores.

A bench shared by two people.

In HICO-DET image 00001195, the sitting hypotheses of two people direct observation to a shared crop containing the supporting bench. Observation recovers the bench, and both sitting relations use its selected grounding. One person-bench pair is retained through the observation association and the other through visual pair assessment, illustrating their complementary contributions to relation coverage.

The same observation supplies an alternative suitcase box. Comparing both candidates against the acquired views, geometric adjudication selects the original box as the shared grounding for subsequent relation verification.

A small food target.

In V-COCO image 18193, the eating hypothesis directs observation to a small sandwich omitted from the initial participant set. The recovered sandwich is verified as the target of both holding and eating, showing how observation guided by one interaction can support another action involving the same participant. Table 41 gives the corresponding action, visibility, and binding factors.

Grounded multi-label verification.

For the person-book pair in HICO-DET image 00000116, the selected boxes, full image, and public action definition specify the visual question: whether the person holds the book. The MLLM assesses this question over {false, true, unknown}. Normalizing the first-token logits by Equation 2 gives a holding score of 0.9859. A separate reading question over the same participants gives 0.9796 (Table 39). Independent action assessments therefore retain both interactions on the shared groundings. Table 41 presents the corresponding factor composition for V-COCO roles.

F.2 Pair Retention in a Distant Gaze Relation

Distant gaze.

V-COCO image 2473 contains an annotated gaze relation between two people. The observer and target boxes match their annotations at IoU 0.9560 and 0.9517. Although the agent and role-state questions favor looking and a visible target, the pair question assigns its highest support to false (Table 40). Neither discovery nor observation associates this pair. Equation 4 therefore excludes it from the binding domain, and no physical look/obj prediction is produced for that pair.

In this example, pair selection excludes the gaze relation despite accurate participant localization. In the shared-bench example, observation associations and visual pair assessment retain different person-bench pairs, illustrating how their combination extends the relations available for verification.

F.3 Shared Geometry and Distinct Semantic Roles

Object and instrument in hitting.

In V-COCO image 579060, initial localization identifies the person, racket, and ball. The racket is both a held object and the instrument of hitting, while the ball fulfills the object role of hitting. The two hitting roles share action evidence, with separate visibility and binding questions identifying their respective targets (Table 41).

Object and instrument in cutting.

V-COCO image 468608 similarly distinguishes a knife as the cutting instrument and a cake as the object being cut. Both are available from initial localization, and their role predictions combine shared action evidence with target-specific assessments. The knife also participates in holding, illustrating the use of one grounding across different action-role assignments.

Appendix G Prompts and Visual Questions

We provide the prompt instructions used for perception and relation verification. Each prompt incorporates the relevant participants, image views, and public interaction definitions.

G.1 Participant Localization

Initial localization receives the full image and public object vocabulary and returns categories, boxes normalized to [0,1000][0,1000], and appearance references:

Localize the people and identifiable targets involved in the scene’s interactions. Organize the output by interaction group: list one person and all associated targets immediately after that person, then proceed to the next person. Cover holding, using, riding, sitting or leaning, wearing, carrying, caring, and person-to-person interactions. Include identifiable nearby objects that may support no-interaction assessment, while prioritizing interaction participants over unrelated background objects.

Give one box for each complete visible instance and include each instance once. A person’s box should cover the visible person; an object’s box should cover the object itself. Describe each reference through visible appearance and position. Return the instance category, normalized box, and reference in the requested format.

G.2 Interaction Discovery and Observation Planning

Discovery receives the full image, initial entities, designated human group, and public interaction definitions. The prompt requests hypotheses, additional participants, and observation regions:

Inspect every designated human. Give concise visible evidence and identify the interactions involving that person. A person can perform several actions and interact with several targets. Use existing instance identities when their targets are already localized. Add an omitted, visually identifiable participant with its category, full-image box, and appearance reference. For role-based actions, distinguish the target fulfilling each object or instrument role.

Examine held, worn, ridden, supporting, and distant visible targets. When the target cannot yet be localized reliably, retain its description and formulate a question for closer observation. Propose up to two regions, giving priority to unlocalized targets and then incomplete instance boundaries. Each request identifies the human, possible action and role, known target when available, target description, localization question, image region, and priority. The region should support localization of the complete visible instance. When the existing view resolves participant localization, return no observation request.

G.3 Targeted Observation

Observation receives a crop, the target description, and the local instances eligible for refinement. Output coordinates are normalized within the crop:

Use this crop and target description to localize the relevant participants. Identify changes to the eligible instances and any additional visible participants. For an existing instance, retain its identity and report the changed category or box. Instances crossing the crop boundary provide context; update complete-instance boxes for eligible identities whose extents lie within the view.

Describe newly identified participants with complete visible-instance boxes and categories. Preserve the distinction between a person and the object they hold or use. Localize visible extent without extrapolating occluded boundaries. Return instance updates and new participants. If the observation provides no reliable localization change, return empty changes.

Returned boxes are mapped to the full image by Equation 9.

G.4 Geometric Adjudication

The geometry question receives the candidate category-and-box descriptions, full image, and acquired crops. Each candidate is assigned an answer letter:

Compare the candidate descriptions of this instance against the image evidence. Select the candidate that best matches its identity, category, and complete visible boundary. For a person, assess the full visible person rather than a hand or torso. For an object, assess the extent of that object rather than its contact region with another participant. Judge localization correspondence; the candidate order does not indicate quality. Answer with the letter of the selected candidate.

Candidate supports are normalized by Equation 2, and the grounding is selected by Equation 3.

G.5 Grounded Relation Questions

Shared instruction.

Relation questions receive the selected participants, action or role definition, and corresponding image views. They share the following instruction:

Assess the specified instances from the image evidence. Use the given boxes to identify the person and target, and verify that those instances correspond to the visual question. Distinguish this person’s action from another person’s action and this target from another instance of its category. An interaction requires visual evidence beyond proximity or the object’s typical use. Multiple actions can hold for the same participants. Apply the supplied action and role meanings and answer with one word from the designated answer set.

Table 42 lists the question types and answer sets.

Pair assessment.

The pair question asks whether any legal positive interaction is visually supported. Its answers denote support for at least one relation (true), rejection of all such relations (false), or unresolved evidence (unknown). Pair retention follows Equation 4, combining this assessment with discovery and observation associations.

No-interaction and action assessment.

No-interaction assessment verifies the participants’ identity and geometry together with the absence of legal positive interactions. Each positive-action question evaluates a specific predicate under its supplied definition: for example, hold concerns bodily or manual support of the target, and read concerns engagement with its textual content. Each question produces a separate false/true/unknown distribution.

Role visibility and binding.

Conditional on the action, visible denotes a localizable role target in the image, including one absent from the entity set; missing denotes the absence of such a target; and unknown denotes unresolved visibility. Binding assesses whether the specified instance fulfills the object or instrument role.

G.6 Public Role Definitions

Table 42 gives the complete target meanings used in V-COCO questions. The role keys follow the benchmark representation. In particular, point/instr denotes the target indicated by the pointing gesture. Action definitions complement these role meanings by specifying the person’s activity: holding a phone and talking on a phone are assessed separately; standing on a board does not alone establish riding or jumping; and skiing, snowboarding, skateboarding, and surfing retain their distinct activity meanings. HICO-DET questions follow the public verb-object taxonomy, with definitions distinguishing predicates such as cut and cut_with, sit_at and sit_on, and hold and carry.
